## Chapter 1
PLAYING PILGRIMS.

"Christmas won't be Christmas without any presents," grumbled Jo, lying on the rug.

"It's so dreadful to be poor!" sighed Meg, looking down at her old dress.

"I don't think it's fair for some girls to have plenty of pretty things, and other girls nothing at all," added little Amy, with an injured sniff.

"We've got father and mother and each other," said Beth contentedly, from her corner.

The faces brightened, then darkened again as Jo said sadly, "We haven't got father, and shall not have him for a long time." No one said "perhaps never," but all thought of him far away, where the fighting was.

Meg reminded them gently why there were to be no presents: it was a hard winter for every one, and "we can make our little sacrifices, and ought to do it gladly." But each had a dollar; Jo longed for Undine and Sintram, Beth for new music, Amy for Faber’s drawing-pencils. "Mother didn't say anything about our money," said Jo; "let's each buy what we want; I'm sure we work hard enough to earn it."

Then came the grievances: Meg's tiresome pupils; Jo's "nervous, fussy old lady"; Beth's dish-washing and stiff hands; Amy’s schoolmates who "label" your father if he isn't rich. "If you mean libel, say so, and not talk about labels, as if papa was a pickle-bottle," laughed Jo. "Don't be statirical," returned Amy, improving her vocabilary.

"Don't peck at one another, children. Don't you wish we had the money papa lost when we were little, Jo?" sighed Meg. They were happier than the rich King children, they agreed, but Amy reproved: "Jo does use such slang words!" Jo whistled. "Don't, Jo; it's so boyish!" "That's why I do it." "I detest rude, unlady-like girls!" "I hate affected, niminy-piminy chits!" "'Birds in their little nests agree,'" sang peace-maker Beth, and the pecking ended.

"Really, girls, you are both to be blamed," lectured Meg. "You are old enough to leave off boyish tricks, Josephine." "I'm not! and if turning up my hair makes me one, I'll wear it in two tails till I'm twenty," cried Jo, shaking down the chestnut mane. "I hate to think I've got to grow up, and be Miss March, and wear long gowns, and look as prim as a China-aster! It's bad enough to be a girl, anyway, when I like boys' games and work and manners! I can't get over my disappointment in not being a boy; and it's worse than ever now, for I'm dying to go and fight with papa, and I can only stay at home and knit, like a poky old woman!" And Jo shook the blue army-sock till the needles rattled like castanets, and her ball bounded across the room.

"Poor Jo! It's too bad, but it can't be helped; so you must try to be contented with making your name boyish, and playing brother to us girls," said Beth, stroking the rough head at her knee with a hand that all the dish-washing and dusting in the world could not make ungentle in its touch.

"As for you, Amy," continued Meg, "you are altogether too particular and prim. Your airs are funny now; but you'll grow up an affected little goose, if you don't take care. I like your nice manners and refined ways of speaking, when you don't try to be elegant; but your absurd words are as bad as Jo's slang."

"If Jo is a tom-boy and Amy a goose, what am I, please?" asked Beth. "You're a dear, and nothing else," said Meg; no one contradicted, for the "Mouse" was the pet.

As young readers like to know "how people look," we will take this moment to give them a little sketch of the four sisters, who sat knitting away in the twilight, while the December snow fell quietly without, and the fire crackled cheerfully within. It was a comfortable old room, though the carpet was faded and the furniture very plain; for a good picture or two hung on the walls, books filled the recesses, chrysanthemums and Christmas roses bloomed in the windows, and a pleasant atmosphere of home-peace pervaded it.

Margaret, the eldest of the four, was sixteen, and very pretty, being plump and fair, with large eyes, plenty of soft, brown hair, a sweet mouth, and white hands, of which she was rather vain. Fifteen-year-old Jo was very tall, thin, and brown, with a decided mouth, a comical nose, and sharp, gray eyes, big hands and feet, a fly-away look to her clothes, and the uncomfortable appearance of a girl who was rapidly shooting up into a woman, and didn't like it. Elizabeth—or Beth, as every one called her—was a rosy, smooth-haired, bright-eyed girl of thirteen, with a shy manner, a timid voice, and a peaceful expression, which was seldom disturbed. Her father called her "Little Tranquillity," and the name suited her excellently; for she seemed to live in a happy world of her own, only venturing out to meet the few whom she trusted and loved. Amy, though the youngest, was a most important person,—in her own opinion at least. A regular snow-maiden, with blue eyes, and yellow hair, curling on her shoulders, pale and slender, and always carrying herself like a young lady mindful of her manners. What the characters of the four sisters were we will leave to be found out.

The clock struck six; Beth set mother’s slippers to warm. "They are quite worn out; Marmee must have a new pair." "I thought I'd get her some with my dollar," said Beth. "No, I shall!" cried Amy. "I'm the oldest—" began Meg. "I'm the man of the family now papa is away, and I shall provide the slippers," cut in Jo.

"Let's each get her something for Christmas, and not get anything for ourselves," said Beth. They planned: "A nice pair of gloves," from Meg; "Army shoes, best to be had," from Jo; "Some handkerchiefs, all hemmed," from Beth; "a little bottle of cologne," from Amy. "Put them on the table, and bring her in and see her open the bundles," said Jo.

They spoke of the Christmas play. Jo drilled Amy’s fainting—"Roderigo! save me! save me!"—to small effect; then Don Pedro, Hagar, Roderigo, and Hugo rehearsed with great spirit. Jo gloated over Macbeth—"Is that a dagger that I see before me?" "No, it's the toasting fork, with mother's shoe on it," cried Meg, and the rehearsal ended in laughter.

"Glad to find you so merry, my girls," said a cheery voice. Mrs. March came in, motherly and noble, the gray cloak and plain bonnet covering "the most splendid mother in the world." She settled into the easy-chair with Amy on her lap, while the others flew about. "I've got a treat for you after supper," she said; at which there was "A letter! a letter!" and three cheers for father. It was cheerful and hopeful, full of camp news; and at the end: "Give them all my dear love and a kiss. Tell them I think of them by day, pray for them by night, and find my best comfort in their affection at all times. A year seems very long to wait before I see them, but remind them that while we wait we may all work, so that these hard days need not be wasted. I know they will remember all I said to them, that they will be loving children to you, will do their duty faithfully, fight their bosom enemies bravely, and conquer themselves so beautifully, that when I come back to them I may be fonder and prouder than ever of my little women."

They sniffed and resolved: Meg would think less of looks and more of work; Amy would not be selfish; Jo would "try and be what he loves to call me, 'a little woman,' and not be rough and wild"; Beth said nothing, but wiped her eyes with the blue army-sock and knitted with all her might.

"Do you remember how you used to play Pilgrim's Progress?" said Mrs. March. Cellar as City of Destruction, roof as Celestial City; lions, Apollyon, bundles tumbling, songs in the sunshine—each recalled a favorite part. "We never are too old for this, my dear... suppose you begin again, not in play, but in earnest," said mother. "We were in the Slough of Despond to-night, and mother came and pulled us out as Help did in the book. We ought to have our roll of directions, like Christian. What shall we do about that?" asked Jo, delighted with the fancy which lent a little romance to the very dull task of doing her duty. "Look under your pillows, Christmas morning, and you will find your guide-book," replied Mrs. March.

They stitched Aunt March’s sheets, naming the long seams Europe, Asia, Africa, and America, and got on capitally. At nine they stopped work and sung, as usual. Beth’s soft touch made music of the old piano; Meg’s voice like a flute led with their mother. Amy chirped; Jo wandered through the airs and came out at the wrong place with a croak that spoilt the most pensive tune.

## Chapter 2
A MERRY CHRISTMAS.

Jo woke first in the gray dawn. No stockings hung at the fireplace; then she remembered, slipped her hand under her pillow, and drew out a little crimson-covered book—"a true guide-book for any pilgrim." She woke Meg, whose green-covered book bore a few words from their mother; Beth and Amy found dove and blue. "Mother wants us to read and love and mind these books," said Meg, and began at once; Jo leaned cheek to cheek and read too; Beth whispered, "How good Meg is! Come, Amy, let's do as they do." "I'm glad mine is blue," said Amy, and the winter sunshine crept in to touch bright heads and serious faces.

"Where is mother?" "Goodness only knows," said Hannah. "Some poor creeter come a-beggin', and your ma went straight off." They looked over the presents. Beth’s handkerchiefs, proudly marked—"Bless the child! she's gone and put 'Mother' on them instead of 'M. March,'" cried Jo—were pronounced "quite sensible" by Meg. Amy slipped in, abashed. "I only meant to change the little bottle for a big one, and I gave all my money to get it, and I'm truly trying not to be selfish any more." The handsome flask, her earnest face—"a trump," said Jo; Beth pinned on her finest rose.

"Merry Christmas, Marmee!" They had just begun when Mrs. March said, "Not far away lies a poor woman with a little new-born baby. Six children are huddled into one bed to keep from freezing... My girls, will you give them your breakfast as a Christmas present?" They were very hungry, but only for a minute. "I'm so glad you came before we began!" cried Jo. "May I go and help carry the things?" asked Beth. Amy heroically took the cream and muffins; Meg covered buckwheats.

The procession set out by back streets. A poor, bare room: broken windows, no fire, ragged bed-clothes, a sick mother, a wailing baby, pale, hungry children. "Ach, mein Gott! it is good angels come to us!" said the poor woman, crying for joy. "Funny angels in hoods and mittens," said Jo, and set them laughing. Hannah made a fire and stopped the panes; Mrs. March fed and comforted the mother and dressed the baby; the girls spread the table and fed the children "like so many hungry birds." "Das ist gut!" "Die Engel-kinder!" they cried, warming purple hands. That was a very happy breakfast, though they didn't get any of it; and when they went away, leaving comfort behind, I think there were not in all the city four merrier people than the hungry little girls who gave away their breakfasts and contented themselves with bread and milk on Christmas morning. "That's loving our neighbor better than ourselves, and I like it," said Meg, as they set out their presents while mother gathered clothes for the poor Hummels. The simple bundles, and the tall vase of red roses and white chrysanthemums, made quite an elegant show. Mrs. March was surprised and touched; slippers on, handkerchief in pocket, rose in her bosom, gloves a "perfect fit"; there was much laughing and kissing and explaining.

The rest of the day went to preparations for the evening. Necessity being the mother of invention, they made everything: pasteboard guitars, antique lamps of butter-boats covered with silver paper, gowns glittering with tin spangles, armor of the same. No gentlemen were admitted; Jo joyfully took male parts, priding herself on a pair of russet-leather boots, an old foil, and a slashed doublet. On Christmas night a dozen girls piled into the "dress-circle;" the bell sounded, curtains flew apart, and "The Witch's Curse, an Operatic Tragedy," began.

"A gloomy wood" and a cave glowed with a small furnace. Hugo the villain stalked in—slouched hat, black beard, mysterious cloak, and the boots—sang of hatred to Roderigo and love for Zara, and summoned, "What ho, minion! I need thee!" Hagar came, promised potions; a rosy spirit sang and dropped a gilded bottle; an ugly black imp croaked and tossed a dark one. Hagar vowed revenge; the curtain fell.

The next set was superb—a tower to the ceiling, lamp at the window, Zara in blue and silver. Roderigo sang a serenade, produced a rope-ladder with five steps, and invited her to descend. "Alas! alas for Zara!" She forgot her train; the tower tottered, leaned, fell with a crash, and buried the lovers. A universal shriek; the russet boots waved from the wreck; a golden head emerged, exclaiming, "I told you so! I told you so!" Don Pedro dragged his daughter out with the aside, "Don't laugh! Act as if it was all right!" and banished Roderigo; the scene went bravely on.

In the castle hall Hagar hid, saw Hugo poison the cups, changed them, and, when the "minion" bore the harmless ones away, set back the deadly draught. Hugo, thirsty after a long warble, drank, clutched and stamped, and fell flat and died, while Hagar sang "in a song of exquisite power and melody." Roderigo, despairing, was saved by a lovely song and a key; he tore off his chains in a spasm of rapture. At last Zara defied the convent, Roderigo demanded her hand, Don Pedro refused because he was not rich—till a letter and a bag from Hagar showered quarts of tin money "till it was quite glorified with the glitter." The stern sire softened; all joined a joyful chorus, and the curtain fell on lovers kneeling to receive his blessing.

Tumultuous applause; then the cot-bed under the "dress-circle" suddenly shut up and extinguished the audience. Roderigo and Don Pedro flew to the rescue, and all came out unhurt, some speechless with laughter. Hannah appeared: "Mrs. March’s compliments, and would the ladies walk down to supper."

It was like Marmee to get up a treat, but anything so fine had not been seen since the days of plenty—ice-cream, pink and white; cake, fruit, French bonbons; and, in the middle, four great bouquets of hot-house flowers. "Is it fairies?" "It's Santa Claus." "Aunt March had a good fit," guessed Jo. "All wrong. Old Mr. Laurence sent it," said Mrs. March. He had heard of their breakfast party and, remembering her father, sent "a few trifles in honor of the day." "That boy put it into his head, I know he did!" cried Jo. She longed to know the Laurence boy who "looks as if he'd like to know us; but he's bashful, and Meg is so prim." Mother liked his manners, had almost asked him in; he looked so wistful, hearing the frolic and having none. "It's a mercy you didn't, mother!" laughed Jo, eyeing her boots. "But we'll have another play some time that he can see. Perhaps he'll help act; wouldn't that be jolly?"

"They are lovely! But Beth's roses are sweeter to me," said Mrs. March, smelling the half-dead posy in her belt. Beth nestled up and whispered, "I wish I could send my bunch to father. I'm afraid he isn't having such a merry Christmas as we are."
